items.source_type: IZA@LISER working paper, full field experiment
items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Related Digital Skills and Employment Outcomes for Underrepresented Women
items.claim: In 1,016 London matched-vacancy tests, an AI-related certificate increased pooled interview invitations for underrepresented women from 11.1% to 14.2% versus a nondigital certificate; the design measured no hires or wages.

items.title: AI Adoption and Firm Size: Employment Effects in Monthly Administrative Data
items.claim: First-time 2023 Danish firm AI adopters had slower employment growth than non-adopters by late 2025, mainly through fewer hires at smaller firms; observational comparison.

items.source_type: Authors’ CEPR exposition of the same working paper
items.title: The adjustment of the Danish labour market to AI has begun
items.claim: Author account gives a roughly 9% trend-relative employment gap by September 2025 and identifies reduced hiring, not layoffs, as the main margin; not independent evidence.

items.source_type: Author-authored exposition of an existing Danish working paper, October 2026
items.title: Still waters, rapid currents: Early labor market transformation under generative AI
items.claim: No differential early-career-share decline at Danish workplaces encouraging chatbots through December 2024 in 11 exposed occupations; not independent evidence from the underlying NBER study.

items.source_type: Federal Reserve FEDS Note, original Lightcast posting analysis, September 2026
items.title: AI on the Factory Floor: Evidence from Manufacturing Job Postings
items.claim: U.S. manufacturing ads increasingly request broad AI skills; unadjusted advertised-pay gaps do not measure worker raises, hires or AI-caused layoffs.

items.title: Generative AI and the Reorganization of Labor Demand
items.claim: U.S. online postings show both cross-role reallocation and within-category listed-task changes in a declining LLM-scored exposure index after 2023Q3. Not observed AI adoption, actual work or job loss.

items.title: Generative AI and Entrepreneurship
items.claim: More exposed existing U.S. startups reduced employment, mainly junior roles; smaller new entrants offset this in aggregate startup employment. Abstract-level result; not a national causal AI estimate.

items.title: Born Small, Staying Small: Generative Artificial Intelligence and the Organization of New Firms
items.claim: UK industry LLM exposure was not associated with a statistically significant firm-entry increase; more exposed new firms had smaller founding teams. Incorporation and directors are not employee counts.

items.source_type: CEPR discussion-paper abstract and author summary
items.title: Prompted to Start: How Generative AI is Transforming Entrepreneurship
items.claim: More GenAI-exposed industries had 20% more startup formation after diffusion, with reported industry-level employment and wage growth from new entry. Abstract-level access does not establish causality or precise labor estimates.

items.source_type: U.S. Census Bureau working paper, September 2026
items.title: AI Exposure and Adoption among U.S. Firms
items.claim: Among matched single-location U.S. firms, occupational AI exposure scores explained about 1–6% of cross-firm variation in reported AI use; the paper does not measure job loss.

items.title: Generative AI and the Redefinition of Entry-Level Software Work
items.claim: U.S. software-developer postings show a roughly 14–15% relative junior-versus-senior decline in the 12 months after ChatGPT’s release and more experience required within some titles. Ads are not hires, and AI attribution is unresolved.

items.title: Who Uses AI? Platform Selection and the Measurement of Occupational AI Exposure
items.claim: Holding a U.S. employment design fixed, changing platform conversation-share inputs changed coefficient size and sometimes sign; workforce reweighting attenuated tested coefficients by 42–93%. This is not a causal AI employment effect.

items.source_type: IZA discussion paper and published journal article
items.title: Does AI Cheapen Talk? Theory and Evidence From Global Entrepreneurship and Hiring
items.claim: Controlled hiring and startup-pitch exercises found 4–9% lower pooled screening accuracy with ChatGPT-assisted pitches on average; a non-English-speaking subgroup showed improved accuracy. No actual hire or employment outcome was measured.

items.source_type: peer-reviewed labor-economics article; official abstract inspected
items.title: Labor Market Signals: The Role of Large Language Models
items.claim: Two cover-letter field experiments reported better letter quality with LLM assistance but no increase in their interview-invitation outcome; modelled matching inefficiency is not observed job loss.

items.source_type: Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland working paper
items.title: The Recent Evolution of AI-Related Labor Demand
items.claim: More LLM-exposed U.S. occupations had higher posted wages but lower real wages for continuously employed workers in the later post period; exposure-based comparisons do not isolate AI causation.

items.title: Voice AI in Firms: A Natural Field Experiment on Automated Job Interviews
items.claim: At one Philippine recruiting firm, eligible entry-level customer-service applications were randomized across interview modes. AI voice interviews increased offer rates by 12% relative to human interviews, with human hiring decisions retained. This does not identify net employment effects.

items.title: Can Labor Markets Function in the Age of AI? The Evaluation Bottleneck in Hiring
items.claim: A formal model predicts that AI-assisted application materials can become less informative about fit, leading employers to rely more on prior experience and potentially reducing screening opportunities for inexperienced but compatible applicants. It does not measure real applicants, employers, interviews, offers, hires, wages, employment or layoffs.

items.title: AI Exposure Isn’t Squeezing Advertised Pay in the US — It’s Boosting It
items.claim: In U.S. job postings with advertised salaries, pay rose faster in the most AI-exposed occupations, while their entry-level share fell sharply. The exposure-based analysis does not prove employer adoption or causation.

items.source_type: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas research analysis
items.title: AI plays a role in weak labor market for college graduates
items.claim: Texas public-university graduates from more generative-AI-automatable majors had lower first-year Texas employment and earnings after ChatGPT’s release. The study measures a regional exposure-by-time association, not observed employer adoption, a personal forecast or a national layoff result.

items.source_type: Stanford Digital Economy Lab working paper
items.title: How Does AI Change Labor Demand? Evidence from 41 Countries
items.claim: A 41-country instrumented study classifies company GenAI job advertisements as adoption and estimates a lower junior employment share plus higher senior employment at adopting multinational affiliates by March 2026. It is an adoption-linked workforce-composition result, not a mass-layoff count or economy-wide employment finding.

items.title: Tracking the Impact of AI on the Labor Market
items.claim: In its September 15 update using August 2026 CPS microdata, Yale Budget Lab finds no clear AI-related U.S. labor-market disruption in its occupational churn, unemployment-exposure, AI-use and synthetic exposure-comparison measures. This limits an economy-wide jobs-collapse claim but does not establish that narrower or later effects are absent.

items.title: The Effects of Artificial Intelligence on Jobs: Evidence from an AI Subsidy Program
items.claim: Among Swedish firms applying for first-time AI-project grants, awardees became more likely to post vacancies five years later, especially white-collar vacancies. The study did not find statistically detectable effects on total employment, hiring or separations. It identifies a grant effect, not a universal generative-AI effect.

items.title: Economic Scenarios for Transformative AI
items.claim: A 4% decline in cognitive employment by 2030 appears in one conditional “substantial change” scenario. It is model output, not an observed 2026 job-loss result or a stated-probability forecast.

items.title: AI Adoption and Firm Size: Employment Effects in Monthly Administrative Data
items.claim: Danish firms first reporting AI use in 2023 had employment growth 11% below non-adopters by late 2025 relative to prior trends, driven by lower recruitment and concentrated in smaller firms. This is an adoption-linked association, not proof that AI alone caused the gap or an economy-wide employment result.

items.title: AI and the Labor Market
items.claim: In its August 2026 update, California’s tracker reports modest declines in three-month initial unemployment-insurance claims from high-exposure occupations under both potential-exposure and observed-use measures, within recent fluctuations. It groups claims by occupation rather than identifying employer AI adoption.

items.title: The Early Impacts of AI on Employment among Recent College Graduates
items.claim: Using U.S. CPS microdata, the paper finds no statistically significant summer-2026 relative unemployment spike among recent college graduates. It is a short-run unemployment result, not an employer-adoption estimate or a measure of first-job quality.

items.source_type: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas research analysis
items.title: Job postings show early signs of AI automation impact
items.claim: Texas online postings fell relatively more in occupations with more generative-AI-automatable tasks after ChatGPT. This is a regional, exposure-linked online-demand result, not a causal estimate of firm adoption, layoffs or national employment.

items.source_type: Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research working paper
items.title: Job Loss Fears in the First Years of Generative Artificial Intelligence
items.claim: The working-paper summary reports no statistically significant response in postings or layoffs for more-exposed occupations, limiting any claim that the Texas result is already a national outcome.

items.title: Labor Market Consequences of Generative AI: Early Evidence from Norway
items.claim: Population-wide Norwegian records find no robust statistically significant employment displacement for young workers in highly exposed occupations; longer pre-trends and backdated placebos weaken a simple post-ChatGPT story.

items.title: AI adoption, productivity and employment: Evidence from European firms
items.claim: A pooled 2019–2024 firm study reports higher labor productivity and no adverse firm-level employment effect in its instrumented AI-adoption specification; it is broader than generative AI and does not measure entry routes.

items.source_type: Ramp Economics Lab and Revelio Labs working-paper presentation
items.title: Does AI eliminate jobs? Economists find heavy adopters hire more.
items.claim: A company-authored firm-data study reports that high-intensity U.S. AI spenders grew total and entry-level headcount after adoption, but it does not establish causation because adopters differed before adoption and the data are proprietary.

items.source_type: Stanford Digital Economy Lab research update
items.title: No Widespread Displacement, but the AI Employment Gap for Young Workers Has Widened to 19%
items.claim: A revised ADP payroll analysis finds a large, widening early-career employment gap by AI exposure but explicitly describes it as descriptive rather than causal.

items.title: The Broken Ladder: AI, Remote Work, and Early-Career Hiring
items.claim: A cross-country study finds remote-work exposure remains predictive of lower junior hiring after joint estimation while its GenAI-exposure coefficient often attenuates, creating an attribution challenge.

items.title: Graduating into Disruption: Labor Market Outcomes for AI-Exposed College Majors
items.claim: Graduates from the most AI-exposed majors had lower initial employment and full-quarter earnings after ChatGPT’s release, but the exposure-based design cannot rule out every coincident field-specific shock.

items.title: Do Job Postings Show Early Labor Market Effects of AI?
items.claim: Broad U.S. job-posting data provide little indication of a distinct AI-driven decline in labor demand since ChatGPT’s release, despite slower overall hiring.

items.title: What Work Does Generative AI Do?
items.claim: U.S. worker survey data show widespread but shallow task-level AI use and demonstrate that occupational exposure is an incomplete proxy for adoption.

items.title: You’re (not) Hired: Artificial Intelligence and Early Career Hiring in the Quarterly Workforce Indicators
items.claim: Early-career hiring and employment declined relative to less-exposed industry-state cells after ChatGPT’s launch; the paper identifies unresolved pandemic-era and exposure-related confounding.

items.title: The Microstructure of AI Diffusion: Evidence From Firms, Business Functions, and Worker Tasks
items.claim: In the late-2025 to early-2026 survey window, most AI-using firms reported task augmentation only and few reported an AI-related employment decrease.

items.title: Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI
items.claim: Danish linked records show task reorganization but no detectable earnings or recorded-hours effect larger than 2% over two years.

items.title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure
items.claim: One in four workers globally are in occupations with some generative-AI exposure; this is a task-exposure estimate, not observed job loss.
